summary: Defines the protocol used between an IRC client and server, assuming the reader knows the IRC architecture. It covers how users connect, send messages and issue commands. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This is the set of words your chat program uses to talk to a chat server, like how to say hello, send a message and ask to join a room.

subtitle: The text-line commands an IRC client sends to a server to register, join channels, chat and query the network.

tldr.problem: A chat client needs one precise, simple language for talking to an IRC server: how to identify itself, join channels, send messages and ask questions about the network.
tldr.mechanism: Clients and servers exchange text messages of up to 512 characters, each made of an optional prefix, a command and up to fifteen parameters. The RFC defines the grammar, the commands (NICK, USER, JOIN, PRIVMSG, MODE and many more) and the numeric replies that answer them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1459 and changed the client protocol very little in order to stay compatible with old clients. It notes that the IRC software, version 2.10, was the only complete implementation at the time.

today: RFC 2812 is an Informational memo from April 2000 that updates RFC 1459. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works together with RFC 2811 for channels and RFC 2813 for the server side.

sections.title: Labels and Who Talks to Whom
sections.content:
This document defines the client protocol and assumes the reader knows the IRC architecture in RFC 2810. The simplest client is any socket program that can connect to a server. The protocol is meant for client-to-server connections only.

Everything has a unique label. A server has a name of at most sixty three (63) characters. A user has a unique nickname of at most nine (9) characters, although clients SHOULD accept longer strings in case future versions allow them. A service is named by a nickname plus a server name. A channel name begins with an ampersand, hash, plus or exclamation mark and is up to fifty (50) characters. The rules for channels themselves live in RFC 2811.

A special class of users, operators, may perform network maintenance such as disconnecting and reconnecting servers. The RFC calls their power to force a user off the network the most controversial one and says its abuse is both destructive and annoying.
sections.eli5: Everyone on the network needs a name nobody else has. People get short nicknames, rooms get names that start with a symbol, and a few grown-ups called operators can look after the network.

sections.title: Message Format and Replies
sections.content:
The protocol uses 8-bit octets with no specific character set, though it is mostly usable from a US-ASCII terminal and a telnet connection. Because of IRC's Scandinavian origin, the characters {}|^ are the lower case equivalents of []\~, which matters when comparing nicknames and channel names.

Each message has up to three parts: an optional prefix (a leading colon plus the true origin), a command, and at most fifteen (15) parameters, all separated by single spaces. The command is either a valid IRC command or a three-digit number. A message ends with CR-LF and MUST NOT exceed 512 characters including the CR-LF, so there are 510 characters for the command and its parameters. There is no continuation line. Empty messages are silently ignored.

Most messages generate a reply of some kind, most often a numeric reply used for both errors and normal replies. Clients should not wait forever for a reply, because client-to-server and server-to-server communication is essentially asynchronous. Section 5 lists the numeric replies, from 001 RPL_WELCOME to error codes such as 433 ERR_NICKNAMEINUSE.

Where wildcards are allowed the string is a mask. The question mark matches exactly one character and the asterisk matches any number of characters, and both can be escaped with a backslash.
sections.eli5: Every message is one line, like a text message with a length limit. It says who it is from, what to do, and any details. The server answers with numbered replies, a bit like a form letter with a code on top.

sections.title: Connecting and Registering
sections.content:
A client registers with a server using a few commands. PASS is optional but MUST come before the later of the NICK/USER pair (for a user) or SERVICE (for a service). The RECOMMENDED order is PASS, NICK, then USER. On success the client gets an RPL_WELCOME (users) or RPL_YOURESERVICE (services) carrying its full client identifier.

NICK gives a nickname or changes it. USER sets the username and real name; its mode parameter is a bitmask where bit 2 sets mode w and bit 3 sets mode i. OPER takes a name and password to gain operator privileges. A user changes their own modes with MODE, but a user attempt to give themselves +o or +O SHOULD be ignored, and the a (away) flag is set only through AWAY.

A session ends with QUIT, and the server replies with an ERROR message. SQUIT lets operators disconnect a server link. KILL closes a client connection; servers generate it on nickname collisions, and the RFC recommends that only operators be allowed to use it and that not even operators should kill users on remote servers.
sections.eli5: When you walk into the chat building you say a secret word if there is one, tell them your nickname, and then give your real name. The server says welcome, and when you leave you say goodbye.

sections.title: Channels and Sending Messages
sections.content:
Channel commands are requests the server grants or denies; they are not available to services. JOIN asks to listen to one or more channels, with optional keys, and the special argument 0 leaves every channel. After a successful join the user receives the topic and a list of members. PART leaves channels and is always granted. MODE queries or changes channel characteristics, with a limit of three (3) changes per command for modes that take a parameter. TOPIC views, sets or clears the topic. NAMES and LIST list visible members and channels. INVITE and KICK bring in or forcibly remove users.

Only PRIVMSG, NOTICE and SQUERY actually deliver text from one client to another; the other commands just make this possible. PRIVMSG targets a nickname, a channel, or a host or server mask (the mask forms are only for operators). NOTICE works the same way but automatic replies MUST NEVER be sent in response to it, which avoids loops between clients that answer each other automatically.

For INVITE, only the inviter and the invited user are notified. Other channel members are not, which the RFC says is occasionally the source of trouble for users.
sections.eli5: To chat in a room you ask to join, then say things to the room. A 'notice' is a message that is not allowed to get an automatic answer, so two robots cannot talk to each other forever.

sections.title: Queries, Optional Commands and Flood Limits
sections.content:
Server query commands return information about any server on the network. They include MOTD (message of the day), LUSERS (size statistics), VERSION, STATS, LINKS, TIME, TRACE, ADMIN and INFO. Where a target parameter appears, wildcard masks are usually valid. User queries are WHO, WHOIS and WHOWAS, and services are listed with SERVLIST.

PING tests whether the other end of a connection is alive and must be answered with PONG as soon as possible. A connection that does not answer within a set time is closed.

Section 4 lists optional features: AWAY, REHASH, DIE, RESTART, SUMMON, USERS, OPERWALL, USERHOST and ISON. The RFC says AWAY is costly in memory and bandwidth, so it SHOULD be used only between client and server, and the user mode a is used to share the status across servers.
sections.eli5: Besides chatting, you can ask the server questions, such as how many people are online or what the news of the day is. A ping is the server tapping you on the shoulder to check you are still awake.

sections.title: Known Problems and Security
sections.content:
The client protocol has almost not evolved since RFC 1459, to keep old clients working. The RFC names a few problems. Nicknames are a finite space, so when two people choose the same one either one fails or both are removed by a server KILL. Wildcard masks cannot escape the escape character, so a mask cannot contain a backslash immediately before a wildcard.

An IESG note warns that the protocol allows several ways of transferring data between clients and that, as with email, the receiver has to be careful how the data is handled. The RFC's own security section does not add detail and instead refers to the server protocol, RFC 2813, because the issues are mostly on the server side. The PASS and OPER passwords are sent in the clear in this protocol.
sections.eli5: There are only so many good nicknames, so fights over names happen. The grown-ups also remind everyone to be careful with anything other people send them.

data.title: Message structure
data.code:
message    =  [ ":" prefix SPACE ] command [ params ] crlf
prefix     =  servername / ( nickname [ [ "!" user ] "@" host ] )
command    =  1*letter / 3digit
params     =  *14( SPACE middle ) [ SPACE ":" trailing ]
           =/ 14( SPACE middle ) [ SPACE [ ":" ] trailing ]
